```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 8.5, fig.height = 6, out.width = "100%")
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
key <- read_csv("outputs/key_numbers.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
kv <- function(m) as.numeric(key$value[key$metric == m])
```

## Introduction

Point a spectrograph at the centre of a nearby galaxy and — around **half the time** —
you will find a **supermassive black hole actively swallowing matter**. That was the
surprise of the *Palomar Spectroscopic Survey of Nearby Galaxies*: in the 1990s,
astronomers used the 200-inch Hale Telescope — then the world's largest — to split the
light of 486 galaxy nuclei into spectra and classify what powered each one (Ho,
Filippenko & Sargent 1995, 1997, 2009).

This report explores the collected data with three questions, all of which turn into
clear, standalone visuals.

## The Three Questions

1. **Can two emission-line ratios separate star-forming galaxies from black holes?**
   The famous **BPT diagram** ([Baldwin, Phillips & Terlevich 1981](https://ned.ipac.caltech.edu/level5/Glossary/Essay_bpt.html));
2. **Does a galaxy's *shape* predict what happens at its centre?** — morphology vs.
   nuclear activity along the Hubble sequence;
3. **Do more massive galaxies host more active nuclei?** — stellar velocity
   dispersion (a black-hole-mass proxy) vs. activity type.

## Data & Methodology

- **Source:** Palomar Spectroscopic Survey, via [VizieR](https://vizier.cds.unistra.fr/viz-bin/VizieR-2?-source=J/ApJS/112/315)
  (Ho, Filippenko & Sargent 1995, 1997, 2009).
- **Probe:** optical emission-line spectra of `r key$value[key$metric=="n_galaxies"]`
  galaxy nuclei taken with the Hale Telescope.
- **Classification:** each nucleus is typed as **H II** (star formation), **Seyfert**
  (luminous AGN), **LINER** (low-ionisation AGN), **Transition** (composite), or
  **Absorption**. `r key$value[key$metric=="n_classified"]` nuclei are classified;
  `r key$value[key$metric=="n_unclassified"]` lack detectable emission lines.
- **BPT ratios:** the dataset's `log_*` columns are *linear* intensity ratios, not
  logarithms — `log10()` is applied here to build the diagram (see `analysis.R`).

```{r classification-table}
classification_counts <- read_csv("outputs/classification_counts.csv",
                                  show_col_types = FALSE)
classification_counts |> knitr::kable()
```

> **Data quality note.** About `r round(100 * as.numeric(key$value[key$metric=="n_unclassified"]) / 486) `% of
> survey galaxies have no emission lines and cannot be classified. Roughly one in
> five classifications is flagged *uncertain* or *very uncertain* — these are drawn
> faded in Figure 1. No physical claims beyond the reported classifications: this is
> a demographics snapshot of the local universe.

## Finding 1 — Two line ratios split star formation from black holes

```{r fig1}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/fig_01_bpt_diagram.png")
```

*Alt text: BPT diagnostic diagram, 406 nuclei, log[NII]/H-alpha on the x-axis and
log[OIII]/H-beta on the y-axis. Points coloured by activity type: blue H II galaxies
form a cloud at lower left; red Seyferts a spur at upper right; orange LINERs scatter
to the right; green transitions sit between. Two dashed boundary curves cut the plane;
uncertain galaxies are paler.*

The diagram works like a referee: it separates **photoionisation by young stars**
(H II regions) from **photoionisation by a black hole's accretion disk** (AGN). The
*ionising power* axis (y) is what does the heavy lifting:

- **Seyfert nuclei** cluster at the top — median `r round(as.numeric(key$value[key$metric=="bpt_med_seyfert"]), 2)` in
  log[OIII]/Hβ, the signature of hard, energetic radiation;
- **H II galaxies** sit at the bottom-left at `r round(as.numeric(key$value[key$metric=="bpt_med_hii"]), 2)` — soft,
  stellar radiation;
- **LINERs** occupy the right-hand side: enough gas to glow, but too little ionising
  power to be a classic active nucleus.

The dashed boundaries (Kauffmann 2003 / Kewley 2001) are theoretical limits: nearly
all star-forming galaxies fall *below* the blue line, and *above* the purple line
star formation is no longer a plausible engine.

## Finding 2 — Shape predicts destiny

```{r fig2}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/fig_02_hubble_sequence.png")
```

*Alt text: 100% stacked horizontal bars along the Hubble sequence (Elliptical,
Lenticular, Spiral, Barred spiral, Irregular). Segments coloured by activity type,
with per-cell galaxy counts labelled. Early-type galaxies are dominated by orange
LINER segments; late types by blue H II.*

| Morphology        | Dominant nucleus   | Share   |
|:------------------|:-------------------|:--------|
| Elliptical        | LINER (AGN)        | **73%** |
| Lenticular (S0)   | LINER / Transition | 42% / 34% |
| Spiral            | H II (star-forming)| **59%** |
| Barred spiral     | H II               | 55%     |
| Irregular         | H II               | 100%    |

Scrolling along the Hubble sequence, the galaxy's *soul* changes: **early-type,
gas-poor systems (E, S0) host quiet, low-luminosity AGN (LINERs), while late-type,
gas-rich systems (spirals, irregulars) are full of young stars**. This is a
demographics result of the local universe — most galaxies are either "asleep
giants" or "star factories", with relatively few in between.

## Finding 3 — Bigger galaxies, busier black holes

```{r fig3}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/fig_03_mass_ladder.png")
```

*Alt text: vertical violin plots of stellar velocity dispersion (log scale) by
activity type, ordered H II, Transition, Seyfert, LINER. Filled by activity colour
with jittered points; white dots mark medians (70, 135, 149, 167 km/s). Dispersion
rises from H II to LINER.*

The **M-sigma relation** ties a galaxy's central black-hole mass to its stellar
velocity dispersion: measure σ and you have a handle on the black hole. Splitting the
sample by activity reveals a clean ladder:

- **H II (star-forming)** nuclei live in the *lightest* galaxies — median
  `r key$value[key$metric=="sigma_hii"]` km/s;
- **LINER** nuclei, in the *heaviest* — median `r key$value[key$metric=="sigma_liner"]` km/s;
- **Seyferts** and transitions sit between
  (`r key$value[key$metric=="sigma_seyfert"]` and
  `r key$value[key$metric=="sigma_transition"]` km/s).

More massive galaxy → more massive black hole → a more energetic (or at least more
recognisable) active nucleus. Exactly the demographics the Palomar team reported by eye
in 1997, now visible in one panel.

## The Big Picture

Put the three figures back together: **black holes are not rare**. Around
`r round(100 * as.numeric(key$value[key$metric=="n_agn_any"]) / as.numeric(key$value[key$metric=="n_classified"]))`%
of nearby galaxies show some AGN signature (Seyfert, LINER, or transition) against
**`r round(100 * as.numeric(key$value[key$metric=="n_hii"]) / as.numeric(key$value[key$metric=="n_classified"]))`%**
pure star formation. The engine sits in the galaxy's centre, and how we see it depends
on *how massive* the system is and *how much gas* is left to feed it.

## Reproducibility

- `analysis.R` — full pipeline: cleaning, morphology binning, and all three figures.
- `outputs/` — `key_numbers.csv` (all headline statistics) and `hubble_strip.csv`.
- `figures/*.png` — the three charts above.
- Data: `palomar_survey.csv`, `palomar_emission_lines.csv`
  (TidyTuesday 2026-08-11, via VizieR).

Run everything with:

```{r repro, eval = FALSE}
source("analysis.R")   # regenerates outputs/ and figures/
```
